Statement of Abbie Strout-Bentes, Executive Director, SAFE Maine to the Health and Human Services Committee in support of LD 143: An Act to Improve Women's Health and Economic Security by Funding Family Planning Services March 10, 2025
Dear Senator Ingwersen, Representative Meyer, and members of the Joint Standing Committee on Health and Human Services,
I am submitting testimony of behalf of Safe Abortions For Everyone, also known as SAFE Maine; we are Maine's abortion fund. We urge committee members to vote in favor of LD 143: An Act to Improve Women's Health and Economic Security by Funding Family Planning Services.
Our mission is to provide financial support to individuals traveling to, living in, or from Maine who need assistance paying for their abortion and associated costs, such as transportation, lodging, childcare, and lost wages. We provide funding for people who are uninsured, those whose insurance doesn't cover abortion care, and people who are unable to use their insurance. Mainers who need abortion care, particularly those who depend on our funding for care, also need access to free or reduced cost sexual and reproductive healthcare services provided by Maine's family planning network. We believe that bodily autonomy is a human right, and when individuals can access essential and basic health care services at family planning care sites across the state they are able to make decisions about their bodies and futures.
Funding Maine's family planning network is a key part of building the future we believe in and one that all Mainers' deserve. A future where all of us - no matter our income or what part of the state we live in - are able to get the healthcare we need, close to home and with healthcare providers we trust. Their network ensures annually that over 30,000 Mainers are able to access the sexual and reproductive health care they need. These services allow us to plan our families and futures, get tested and treated for sexually transmitted infections, and receive gender-affirming care, our annual cancer screenings, and other preventative care. With a half-century of experience and 60 locations across our state, the family planning network is a trusted lifeline in our communities. For many individuals who get their care within the family planning network, it is their only source of healthcare annually, highlighting the network's significant impact on public health and individual well-being.
It is already too hard to get healthcare in our state, and if family planning care is not funded, the consequences will be devastating for communities, resulting in fewer people receiving care. Now is the time to invest in the health and wellness of Maine's communities by supporting LD 143.
Sincerely,
Abbie Strout-Bentes

uncertain political landscape. LD 143, An Act to Improve Women's Health and Economic Security by Funding Family Planning
Services, will help safeguard Maine's family planning network so that the most vulnerable people in our state can access the essential healthcare they need.

The care provided includes birth control, cancer screenings, routine gynecological exams and care, testing and treatment for sexually transmitted infections, and gender~aff|rming care, as well as behavioral health services, vaccinations, nutrition support, and well person care.

Maine's family planning care network consists of 19 Maine Family Planning health centers, 4 Planned Parenthood health centers, 32 Federally-Qualified Health Centers, and 8 School-based health centers. These providers offer millions of dollars in free and reduced-cost care each year, but for the last decade state funding has remained fixed at a flat rate representing a fraction of the actual cost. Family planning services are critical for women, couples, and families of every size to stay healthy and thriving. Throughout my life I have needed safe, affordable, and convenient reproductive health access for a number of reasons, and to go without it would have put my life on a much different trajectory.
For a decade I used a birth control pill both to avoid unplanned pregnancy and to help manage painful PMS symptoms. As part of my routine care, in my early 20s I had an abnormal pap smear that required a colposcopy and biopsy. This was caught early, so the biopsy was sufficient to remove any areas of concern. I will never know if, left undetected, that might have grown into cancer. I would not have gone out of my way for a pap smear at that stage of life, so having routine access to gynecological care potentially prevented a life threatening issue.
Years later, my husband and I decided to take "next steps" with our lives. Through careful planning and saving we were able to buy a house in Gorham in late 2020. Despite being in the Portland area, the only medical appointment I could get within months of moving was a family planning appointment. As a healthy young person, PCP access was secondary compared to maintaining my birth control until we were ready, and then when ready, to safely get pregnant. Waiting until then meant we both had established successful careers and a lovely home and community. I'm grateful then for the excellent care we received through my conception and pregnancy journey, amid some complications, as it resulted in our beloved, healthy daughter (now 2 years old).
Post pregnancy of course it is critical to get access again to safe and effective birth control methods, for the health of the mother as well as any future children. Once again, access to these services helped me navigate an unexpectedly tricky health landscape. I first had an IUD inserted, but that resulted in some complications which necessitated we remove it only a few months later. From there I went back to my "safe" birth control pill, which had worked well for a decade pre-pregnancy, but post-pregnancy bodies are different! Over time that caused some serious new health concerns including unsafe migraines. Yet again I needed to adjust my birth control method under the care of my doctor.
Having safe and accessible family planning and reproductive health care access supports families like mine to be healthy, at the size we want, with children we can provide for and dote on. I hope every family in the state maintains access to the services I've been grateful to receive.

Thank you Chair Ingwersen, Chair Meyer and distinguished members of the Health and Human Services committee. I am Representative Katrina Smith and I represent District 62. I am here today to testify Ought not to Pass on LD 143 and detail why this is the wrong action for Maine.

We stand at a critical moment in Maine's history--a moment where the places where life begins, our birthing centers, are vanishing across the state. This is not just a statistic or a headline; it's a reality that's reshaping our communities, especially in our rural areas, and it demands our attention. Today, I want to talk about where this is happening, why it's happening, and why we must shift our focus to investing in the children we already have rather than pouring resources into new family planning services as this bill requests.

Let's start with the facts. Over the past decade, nine hospitals in Maine have either closed their birthing units or announced plans to do so. These closures span the state, hitting rural communities the hardest. In 2022, St. Mary's Regional Medical Center in Lewiston shut its birthing unit. In 2021, it was Bridgton Hospital. Before that, in 2018, Calais Regional Hospital ceased offering labor and delivery services, and in 2015, Penobscot Valley Hospital in Lincoln followed suit. More recently, in 2023, we saw closures announced in York, Rumford, and Fort Kent. And just this year, in 2025, Northern Light Inland Hospital in Waterville suspended its birthing services as of March 1st, while Waldo Hospital in Belfast is set to end theirs in April. These aren't just buildings closing their doors--these are lifelines being cut for families across Maine.

Why is this happening? The reasons are consistent and troubling. Hospital administrators point to three main challenges: difficulty hiring staff, a declining number of births, and reimbursement rates that don't cover the high, fixed costs of keeping a birthing unit open. Northern Light Health cited ongoing recruiting challenges for labor and delivery providers as the reason for closing Inland Hospital's unit in Waterville. In rural areas like Fort Kent and Rumford, some hospitals were handling fewer than 100 births a year, far below the national standard of 200 deliveries needed to sustain expertise and safety. Add to that shortages of pediatric providers, anesthesia coverage, and nurses, and you see a system stretched beyond its breaking point.

The impact is stark. Rural Mainers now face an average 45-minute drive--one way--to the nearest birthing hospital, the longest such travel time in New England. For high-risk pregnancies, that journey can stretch to Bangor, Portland, or even Boston. Yet every time a birthing unit closes, we're telling those families they're on their own. We're forcing mothers to travel miles in labor, risking their health and their babies' lives. Research from other states shows that when birthing services vanish, prenatal care drops, preterm births rise, and maternal mortality triples in so-called "maternal care deserts." We cannot let Maine become one of those deserts.

Instead of sinking money into new family planning initiatives, let's invest in the children we have. That means keeping our remaining birthing centers open by addressing staffing shortages--offering incentives to attract

doctors and nurses to rural Maine and supporting training programs to ensure staff can maintain their skills even with lower birth volumes. It means building a safety net for midwives and home births, so families have options closer to home. My remarks should not be used as facts to promote birth control or family planning centers, but should be seen as a cry for help from those already experiencing hardship in our state.
